questions.q: What is a hormone defined as in human physiology?
a: A chemical substance produced by an endocrine gland, carried by the blood, which alters the activity of one or more specific target organs
An electrical impulse travelling along an axon
An enzyme that speeds up digestion in the stomach
A white blood cell that destroys bacterial pathogens

questions.q: Through which medium are hormones transported from endocrine glands to their target organs?
Which endocrine gland is often referred to as the 'master gland' because it secretes several hormones that control other endocrine glands?
Which hormone is secreted by the adrenal glands during emergency or 'fight or flight' situations?
What is the primary effect of adrenaline on the heart rate?
a: It increases heart rate and stroke volume to pump more oxygenated blood to muscles
It decreases heart rate to conserve energy
It has no effect on cardiovascular activity

questions.q: Which gland produces insulin and glucagon to regulate blood glucose concentration?
What is the role of thyroxine produced by the thyroid gland?
a: To stimulate water reabsorption in the kidneys
To control the basal metabolic rate (the speed at which chemical reactions occur in the body)

questions.q: Which hormone is responsible for the development of male secondary sexual characteristics during puberty?
Which female hormone is responsible for repairing and thickening the uterus lining during the menstrual cycle?
What is the primary role of progesterone during the menstrual cycle and pregnancy?
a: To stimulate egg maturation in ovaries
To maintain and thicken the lining of the uterus, preparing it for implantation and preventing menstruation
To break down the corpus luteum

questions.q: How does hormonal coordination compare to nervous coordination regarding speed and duration of response?
a: Hormonal responses are faster and shorter-lived
Nervous responses are slower and last for weeks
Hormonal responses are generally slower, travel via the blood, and produce longer-lasting effects compared to electrical nerve impulses
Both systems operate at identical speeds

questions.q: Which of the following symptoms is commonly associated with an overactive thyroid gland producing excessive thyroxine (hyperthyroidism)?
a: Slow heart rate and weight gain
Increased metabolic rate, weight loss, and hyperactivity

questions.q: What happens to blood glucose levels immediately after eating a carbohydrate-rich meal?
a: Blood glucose levels rise, triggering the pancreas to secrete insulin
Blood glucose levels drop to zero
Blood glucose levels remain completely unaffected
Adrenaline is released to consume the sugar

questions.q: Which hormone stimulates the liver and muscle cells to convert excess glucose into glycogen for storage?
What is the condition caused by the failure of the pancreas to secrete sufficient insulin, leading to high blood glucose concentrations?
Which of the following is a typical symptom or sign of untreated diabetes mellitus?
a: Low blood sugar and constant sleepiness
High concentration of glucose in the urine and frequent urination

questions.q: What role does the hormone FSH (Follicle-Stimulating Hormone) play in the human reproductive system?
a: It stimulates the development and maturation of an egg follicle in the ovary
It causes the breakdown of the uterus lining

questions.q: Which pituitary hormone triggers ovulation (the release of a mature egg from the ovary)?
Why is plant hormone auxin considered a plant growth substance rather than an animal-like hormone?
a: It is produced in the liver and transported in xylem
It only functions in animal muscles
It is produced in shoot and root tips and affects cell elongation locally or through transport, rather than via an endocrine blood system

questions.q: Which of the following describes a key target organ for adrenaline during a fright reaction?
a: Liver (where glycogen is converted to glucose)

questions.q: What is negative feedback in the context of the endocrine system?
a: A mechanism where a change in a condition triggers a response that counteracts or reverses the change, restoring equilibrium
A process that amplifies a hormone signal indefinitely until cell exhaustion
The complete destruction of hormone molecules in the stomach
The nervous transmission of signals across synapses

questions.q: How does the body respond when blood glucose levels fall too low between meals?
a: The pancreas secretes insulin to absorb more sugar
The pancreas secretes glucagon, which stimulates the liver to break down stored glycogen into glucose and release it into the blood
The pituitary gland stops all blood flow

questions.q: Which of the following endocrine glands is located in the neck and regulates metabolism?
What is plant tropism regulated by?
a: Auxin distribution in response to stimuli like light or gravity

questions.q: Which hormone stimulates the lining of the uterus to develop blood vessels after menstruation ends?
What is the function of the corpus luteum formed in the ovary after ovulation?
a: To produce FSH for egg growth
To secrete progesterone and some oestrogen to maintain the uterine lining

questions.q: Which of the following is an endocrine gland that secretes hormones regulating blood calcium levels and metabolism, situated near the windpipe?
What happens to the pupils of the eyes when adrenaline is released into the bloodstream?
a: Pupils react only to blue light
Pupils dilate to let in more light for better vision in stressful situations

questions.q: Which hormone prepares female secondary sexual characteristics such as widening of hips and breast development during puberty?
What is the primary medical use of synthetic insulin produced using genetically modified bacteria?
a: To treat bacterial infections like pneumonia
To treat Type 1 diabetes by replacing the missing hormone
To lower blood pressure in hypertension

questions.q: Which of the following describes a target organ?
a: An organ that destroys old red blood cells
An organ that possesses specific receptors responding to a particular hormone
An organ that filters metabolic waste

questions.q: Which hormone triggers the thickening of the uterine lining during the second half of the menstrual cycle (days 15 to 28)?
What triggers the start of menstruation (the breakdown of the uterine lining) in the female cycle?
a: A sharp drop in oestrogen and progesterone levels when fertilization does not occur

questions.q: Which of the following organs has both endocrine functions (producing hormones) and exocrine functions (producing digestive enzymes)?
Why is it important that hormones are broken down in the liver and excreted by the kidneys after fulfilling their function?
a: To prevent them from turning into solid fat
To provide energy for muscle contraction
To prevent continuous, unwanted stimulation of target organs

questions.q: What is the primary function of testosterone in males besides secondary sexual characteristics?
a: To stimulate red blood cell destruction
To stimulate sperm production in the testes

questions.q: Which endocrine gland responds directly to blood glucose concentration changes without requiring initial brain nervous stimulation?
What effect does increased levels of thyroxine have on the pituitary gland through negative feedback?
a: It stimulates the pituitary to release more TSH
It inhibits the pituitary gland from releasing TSH (Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone)

questions.q: Which of the following correctly pairs an endocrine gland with its primary hormone?
What causes the physiological changes such as increased breathing rate, increased pulse, and dilated airways during a fright?
a: Secretion of adrenaline into the blood
